n: Right after God’s covenant promise, the chronicler shows it coming true: David subdues the Philistines and takes Gath, the hometown of Goliath.

f.g: One of the five main Philistine cities; 2 Samuel 8:1 calls the conquest “Metheg-ammah.”

n: David defeats Moab, which becomes a tributary state paying yearly gifts.

f.g: Paid tribute—regular payments from a conquered people.

n: David defeats Hadarezer of Zobah, a powerful Aramean (Syrian) kingdom, extending his influence toward the Euphrates—close to the borders God promised Abraham.

f.g: Also spelled Hadadezer, “Hadad (a storm god) is help.”

n: David captures many chariots but disables most of the horses, keeping only enough for a hundred chariots. Israel was not to trust in horses and chariots.

f.g: Hamstrung—cut the leg tendons so the horses could not be used in war.
2 Samuel 8:4 reads 1,700; numbers were easily miscopied.

n: When the Arameans of Damascus come to help Zobah, David defeats them too.

f.g: The Aramean kingdom centered at Damascus.

n: David stations troops in Damascus, and the Arameans pay tribute. The chronicler credits the Lord: He gave David victory wherever he went.

f.w: the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went
f.g: Or “the LORD gave David victory wherever he went.”

n: David brings the gold shields of Hadarezer’s officers to Jerusalem as trophies.

f.g: Ceremonial shields, possibly quivers, a display of wealth.

n: The huge quantity of bronze captured from Zobah’s cities was later used by Solomon for the temple’s bronze sea, pillars and vessels. David’s wars quietly supply God’s house.

f.g: Called Betah and Berothai in 2 Samuel 8:8.

n: Tou, king of Hamath to the north, hears of David’s victory over his enemy Hadarezer.
Tou sends his son with congratulations and rich gifts, seeking friendship with Israel’s rising king.

f.g: To greet him and ask after his well-being—a diplomatic gesture.

n: David dedicates all these treasures to the Lord rather than keeping them. They become a fund for the future temple.
Abishai defeats 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt, probably south of the Dead Sea.

f.g: 2 Samuel 8:13 credits David as king; Psalm 60’s heading mentions Joab. Victories were credited to king and commanders alike.

n: Edom too comes under David’s rule. The refrain repeats: the Lord gave David victory wherever he went.

f.w: all the Edomites became David's servants

n: David reigns over all Israel with justice and righteousness—the ideal of a godly king, foreshadowing the Messiah’s righteous reign.
David’s chief officials are listed: Joab commands the army, and Jehoshaphat keeps the royal records.

f.g: Royal herald or secretary of state, who kept records and announced decrees.

n: Zadok and Abimelech serve as priests; Shavsha is the royal scribe.

f.g: Called Ahimelech in 2 Samuel 8:17; Abiathar also served as priest.
Also called Seraiah or Shisha; perhaps a foreign name.

n: Benaiah commands David’s foreign bodyguard, and David’s sons serve as chief officials. Where 2 Samuel calls David’s sons “priests,” Chronicles uses a term reserving priesthood for Levites.

f.g: Probably Cretans and Philistines—loyal mercenaries in David’s royal guard.
